e.t: The word means “abyss,” naming a distinct realm or depth mentioned in the Greek New Testament. It is used nine times, appearing once in Luke, once in Romans, and seven times in Revelation. Its repeated use in Revelation shows that the term remains an important designation there, while its appearances in Luke and Romans show that it is also used elsewhere in the New Testament. The precise force of the word in any verse depends on that passage’s surrounding text.

me: Verb, Present, Active, Participle, Nominative, Singular, Masculine

e.t: This word means “be distressed” or “to be troubled,” describing a person experiencing serious inner anguish or emotional disturbance. It presents distress as a genuine burden rather than a light concern. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, each in a different verse. Its uses include language for intense personal distress, so the surrounding passage is important for showing what caused the trouble and how the person responded. The word itself focuses on the condition of being deeply troubled.

This word means “eternal.” It describes what belongs to unending duration rather than a temporary period. In the Greek New Testament, it is used 71 times, including descriptions of eternal life, eternal judgment, and what God gives or promises. Its central force remains the same across these uses: it points to something enduring without a stated endpoint. The surrounding passage determines exactly what is being described as eternal in each verse.

The word means “aloes,” the name of a substance. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at John 19:39. Its meaning is straightforward: it identifies aloes rather than an action, quality, or person. The available information supports this ordinary lexical sense, but does not include the surrounding verse text needed to explain the word’s particular significance in that scene. Thus, readers can understand it as a reference to aloes without assigning it an additional meaning beyond that word’s basic sense.

e.t: This word means “to gird,” referring to fastening or gathering clothing around oneself. It is an action word describing preparation by securing what is worn so movement is less hindered. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Peter 1:13. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the basic picture is of making oneself ready by drawing clothing into place.

e.t: This word means “to sail away from” or “to set sail.” It describes leaving a place by ship or beginning a voyage. In the Greek New Testament, it appears four times, all in Acts, and each use concerns travel by sea. The word functions as an action word, focusing on the departure or beginning of a sea journey rather than on the destination or the wider events surrounding the voyage. Its exact force in any particular verse is understood from the surrounding passage.

This word means “with one’s own hand,” describing something done personally and directly rather than through someone else. It emphasizes the person’s own action or involvement. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only once, in Acts 27:19. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning points to personal, hands-on action instead of delegated or indirect activity.

me: Verb, Present, Active, Indicative, third, Plural

e.t: This word means to desecrate or profane—to treat something holy as common, defiled, or unfit for sacred use. It describes an act that dishonors what has been set apart for God. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Matthew 12:5 and Acts 24:6, and is rendered “profane” in both places. Its precise force in either verse is determined by the surrounding passage, but its central idea remains the violation or dishonoring of what is sacred.

“Hill” means a raised area of land, smaller or less imposing than a mountain. In the Greek New Testament, this word occurs twice, both in Luke, and refers to elevated terrain. It is a noun naming a physical feature of the landscape. Its plural form can speak of several hills. The word itself describes the landform; the surrounding verse determines what those hills signify within the passage.

Gennesaret is a proper name for a place mentioned in the Greek New Testament. It is not a description of an action, quality, or person, but a geographical name used to identify a location. The name appears three times in the Greek New Testament: once each in Matthew, Mark, and Luke. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise significance in each passage cannot be explained further; its basic meaning is simply the place-name “Gennesaret.”

This word describes a person held in custody or confinement—a prisoner. It is used of people who are physically detained, including those kept under guard, and can refer to one person or several. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 16 times in 16 verses, with uses appearing from Matthew through Hebrews. Its central meaning remains straightforward: someone whose freedom has been restricted by imprisonment or detention.

me: Verb, second Aorist, Active, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This word means “to stop,” describing the ending or ceasing of an action. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at Luke 7:45, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated biblical examples. As a verb, it expresses that something no longer continues. The precise force in Luke 7:45 depends on the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included here.

This word means “dysentery,” an illness affecting the intestines. It names a physical sickness rather than an action, command, or character quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 28:8. The word identifies the kind of illness involved, while the surrounding verse and passage provide the particular details of the case. Its central meaning remains the medical condition itself: dysentery.【p03:word:greek-nt:G1420:identity】【p03:word:greek-nt:G1420:occurrences】【p01:word:greek-nt:G1420:reference:0】

This word means “praise”: approval or commendation given because someone’s actions or character are recognized as worthy. In the Greek New Testament, it can describe praise directed toward God, honor received by faithful people, or commendation associated with doing what is right. It may also refer to the approval granted by authorities to those who practice good. The word occurs 11 times in the Greek New Testament, showing a recurring idea of recognizing what is good and worthy of approval.

e.t: This word means to come to know or to know something with recognition and understanding. It can describe gaining knowledge, becoming aware of a person or matter, or recognizing what something truly is. Its basic sense is more specific than mere mention: it points to knowledge reached or possessed. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 44 times, so its exact emphasis depends on the sentence where it appears. It is commonly rendered “know,” while “come to know” highlights the movement into understanding.

This word means “remaining”—what is left after something has already been removed, completed, or passed. It points to what continues or is still available, rather than to the whole of something. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Peter 4:2. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its basic meaning is the portion or time still left. It functions as a concise description of what remains after an earlier part has been accounted for.

This Greek New Testament word expresses “enthusiasm” and “wholeheartedness”—an eager, sincere attitude rather than reluctant effort. It describes the spirit or disposition with which someone acts, emphasizing willing engagement. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Ephesians 6:7. Its precise force in that verse is understood from the surrounding sentence and passage, but its central meaning is a genuinely willing and wholehearted response.

e.t: This word means “badly.” It is an adverb, so it describes how something happens or how a person is affected rather than naming a person, place, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 16 times, from Matthew through James. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on the surrounding words, but its central sense remains a description of something taking place badly.

e.t: This word describes overtaking something, taking hold of it, obtaining it, or realizing it. It is a verb expressing the act of reaching, grasping, or coming to possess something, whether physically or in understanding. Its exact force depends on the sentence, but the central idea is gaining hold of or arriving at something. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 15 times, showing repeated use for both overtaking and taking hold. The related sense of realizing highlights coming to understand or recognize something.

This word refers to the smallest stroke or mark in writing, described as “least stroke of a pen” or “tittle.” It points to a tiny written detail rather than a complete letter or larger sign. The word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, in Matthew 5:18 and Luke 16:17. Its basic meaning emphasizes extreme smallness and precision in written form; the surrounding verse determines how that image functions in each passage.

e.t: This word refers to a Corinthian person or group—someone associated with Corinth. It is rendered “Corinthian” or “Corinthians,” identifying people by their connection to that place rather than describing a quality or action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice: once in Acts and once in 2 Corinthians. Its exact role in either passage is determined by the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning is a person or people from Corinth.

This Greek New Testament word means “crying out” or “shouting”—a loud, forceful vocal expression. It focuses on an audible outcry, emphasizing the raised voice rather than ordinary speech. The term appears six times in the Greek New Testament, each time in a different verse. Its central idea remains the same while surrounding context identifies what prompted the outcry and what it communicates.

This word refers to ministry or worship—the service offered in devotion to God. It can describe religious service as an ongoing duty rather than merely an inner belief. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times, including passages that speak of Israel’s sacred privileges, believers offering themselves to God, and the ordered service connected with the tabernacle. Its precise emphasis—ministry or worship—depends on the surrounding sentence.

Lysias is a personal name, identifying someone called Lysias. It is not a word describing an action, quality, or spiritual idea, but a proper name used to identify a person. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Acts: Acts 23:26 and Acts 24:22. The name itself gives the person’s identification; the surrounding passage supplies the details about who he was and what he did.

e.t: This word means “to rave”: to speak or act in a wildly irrational way. It describes behavior viewed as madness or extreme loss of self-control, rather than simply ordinary excitement or strong emotion. In the New Testament, it occurs five times, including passages where people react to Jesus’ words, respond to a reported event, or judge Paul’s preaching. The surrounding verse determines whether the word is being used as an accusation or as a description of behavior. Its basic sense remains the same: conduct that appears irrational or delirious.

This word means honey, the naturally sweet substance produced by bees. It is an ordinary noun naming a food, and its New Testament uses retain that straightforward sense rather than expressing an abstract idea by themselves. The word occurs four times in the Greek New Testament, in Matthew, Mark, and Revelation. In the Gospel accounts it is associated with John the Baptist’s food, while Revelation uses it in connection with something tasted. The surrounding passage determines the significance of each occurrence, but the word itself refers simply to honey.

This word refers either to noon, the middle part of the day, or to the south, the direction opposite north. Its precise sense is determined by the sentence in which it appears. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Acts, showing these two ordinary uses. It can therefore describe a time of day or a direction, rather than expressing an abstract idea or action.

This word is a negative particle meaning “not” or “no,” used to deny, prohibit, or reject something in a sentence. It can also express a negative expectation such as “perhaps” when the surrounding wording calls for that sense. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 1,042 times, so it serves a broad and frequent role in statements, questions, commands, and descriptions. Its exact force depends on the sentence where it appears, but its central function is to mark negation.

This word describes someone who practices the same trade or craft as another person. Its central meaning is “of the same trade,” identifying a shared occupation rather than merely a general similarity. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 18:3. The word therefore points specifically to a person connected with another through the work or craft they both practice.

e.t: This word means “to rush” or “to stampede,” describing sudden, forceful movement. It functions as a verb, presenting people or animals as surging forward rather than moving calmly or slowly. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times, appearing in the Gospels and Acts. The surrounding context determines whether the movement is a wild charge, a frightened surge, or a crowd pressing forward, but the central idea remains rapid, uncontrolled movement toward a direction or place.

e.t: This word means “to make obsolete” or “to make old.” It describes something becoming outdated, worn out, or no longer current rather than remaining fresh and in force. As a verb, it focuses on the process by which something reaches that condition. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, appearing in Luke and Hebrews. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea is clear: something is becoming old or passing out of use.

This Greek New Testament word means “to go on foot” or “to walk,” describing movement made by walking. It names the act of traveling by foot rather than simply indicating arrival or departure. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 20:13. That reference identifies its sole occurrence, while the surrounding verse text is needed to explain how the action functions in that sentence. Its central meaning remains straightforward: walking or proceeding on foot.

This word refers to “speaking many words” or “wordiness”—using an abundance of words rather than expressing something briefly. It names excessive or prolonged speech as a manner of speaking, without by itself describing whether the words are true, false, wise, or foolish. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only once, so its precise force in that sentence depends on the surrounding passage and the way the speaker’s speech is being described.

The word means “thing”: something being considered, discussed, or dealt with. It is broad rather than naming one specific kind of object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 11 times, so its precise sense in any verse comes from the surrounding words and subject. The word itself simply identifies something as a “thing,” whether the sentence concerns an ordinary matter or a significant concern.

e.t: “Recently” means not long ago or in the near past. It is an adverb, so it tells when something happened rather than naming a person, place, or thing. In the Greek New Testament, this word occurs once, in Acts 18:2. Its basic sense marks an event as having happened shortly before the time being discussed. The precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but the word itself points clearly to recent time.

“Early morning” refers to the beginning part of the day, before the day has fully advanced. In the Greek New Testament, this word appears twice, and both occurrences are rendered as morning. It identifies the time of day rather than describing an action, person, or spiritual quality. Its basic meaning is therefore straightforward: the early hours of morning. The surrounding verse determines what happens at that time, but the word itself supplies the time reference.

e.t: “Rooted” describes being firmly established, like something fixed by roots. In the Greek New Testament, this word appears twice, expressing a settled foundation rather than something temporary or easily moved. It describes something planted and remaining established. The word occurs once in Ephesians and once in Colossians. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain its particular use in either passage.

e.t: This word means “to cause to shake” or simply “to shake.” It describes movement produced in something or someone, whether by an external force or by the thing itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times across five verses, including passages in Matthew, Hebrews, and Revelation. Its central idea remains physical disturbance or trembling; the surrounding verse determines what is being shaken and why. The word is used consistently with the ordinary sense of shaking rather than expressing a separate abstract meaning.

This word means “Sinai,” the proper name of a place mentioned in the New Testament. It is not a general description or action word, but a specific place-name. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times: twice in Acts and twice in Galatians. The name appears in Acts 7:30 and 7:38, and in Galatians 4:24–25. Its precise significance in each passage comes from the surrounding verse and argument, but the word itself consistently identifies Sinai.

This word refers to goods seized from a defeated person or enemy—“plunder” or “spoils.” It describes what is taken as the result of victory, rather than the act of fighting itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 11:22, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its central idea remains the valuable possessions captured from someone who has been overcome.

e.t: This word means “to advise” or “to consult”: it describes seeking or giving counsel, often with others involved in deciding what should be done. As a verb, it focuses on the act of conferring or taking advice rather than on the decision’s outcome. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, so its meaning is consistent but its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This word means “such as this.” It points to something that has just been identified or is being described, drawing attention to its particular kind or character. It functions as a concise identifying expression rather than naming a person, place, or action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Peter 1:17. Its exact force in that verse is best understood from the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains a reference to something of this kind.

e.t: This word means “to sail the lee” or “to sail to the lee of”—to steer a vessel along the sheltered side of something, using its protection from the wind. It describes a specific sailing maneuver rather than sailing in general. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Acts 27, where the narrative describes sea travel. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage and the object providing shelter.

This word means “kiss,” referring to the act or expression of kissing. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs seven times across seven verses. Its uses include both an ordinary greeting among believers and a kiss used as a sign of betrayal, so the word itself names the physical act while the surrounding context shows the purpose or meaning attached to it. The same basic sense appears consistently in its New Testament occurrences.

e.t: This word means “to ponder” or “to think”—to give something thoughtful attention in the mind. It describes inward reflection rather than outward speech or action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 10:19, so its exact force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its basic sense is mental consideration: a person is thinking carefully about something, turning it over in the mind, or reflecting on what it may mean.
